title: Not excusing
hookLine: forgiving doesn't mean it was okay

cards: "It's fine." Two small words. Someone apologizes for the missed birthday, the sharp comment in the meeting, the promise that quietly fell through, and out comes the reflex: it's fine, don't worry about it.
Sometimes that's simply true. Sometimes it's a way to end an awkward moment and get back to dinner. And sometimes it isn't fine at all, and saying so would feel like making a scene.
Forgiving someone and telling them it was fine can sound almost the same out loud. Today pulls them apart.

teach.b: Robert Enright, a psychologist who has written about forgiveness, sets out what forgiveness is not. It is not condoning. It is not excusing.
It is not forgetting. His point is almost a matter of logic: you can only forgive something that was actually wrong. If it was fine, there's nothing to forgive.
An old story does this out loud. In Genesis, Joseph's brothers once sold him away. Years later he has power over them, and after their father dies they're terrified he'll finally take revenge.
Listen to the order of what he says: "But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good." He names it first, plainly, to their faces. He doesn't say it was nothing.
Then, in the next verse: "Now therefore fear ye not: I will nourish you, and your little ones." Named, and then let go. Why the naming matters: excusing makes the wrong smaller until it disappears.
Forgiving lets the wrong keep its full size, and releases it anyway. That's harder, and more honest, because the person who was hurt doesn't have to pretend.
On an ordinary Tuesday it sounds like two sentences, both true, said together: that wasn't okay, and I'm letting it go.
Neither cancels the other. The first protects the truth. The second frees the one saying it.

how: In forgiveness counseling based on Robert Enright's work, people first name the wrong done to them and the harm it caused, and only then consider forgiving; forgiveness is taught as distinct from condoning, excusing or forgetting.

o: forgiving a wrong while still naming it as wrong
forgetting the wrong so it can't hurt anymore
deciding the hurt was too small to matter at all

games.q: named, then let go — tap the pairs.

s: forgiving something means agreeing it was okay
you can only forgive something that was actually wrong. if it was fine, there's nothing to forgive.
Joseph names the wrong before he comforts his brothers
"ye thought evil against me" comes first; "fear ye not" comes after.
on Enright's list, forgetting is part of forgiving
he lists forgetting with condoning and excusing, as things forgiveness is not.

games.q: a coworker apologizes for taking credit for your work, and it really wasn't okay. which reply forgives without excusing?
o: "that wasn't okay, and I'm letting it go."
games.why: the honest pair: the wrong keeps its full size, and it's released anyway. Joseph does the same in Genesis 50: "ye thought evil against me," then "fear ye not."

practice: Choose one wrong done to you that you've waved away with "it's fine," and name it in one plain sentence in your head: what they did, and that it wasn't okay, at full size, with no speech.
Let it stand for a few breaths, then, if you're ready, add the second sentence, and I'm letting it go; if you're not ready, the first sentence is enough for today.

wordCard.voice: Not excusing. Forgiving lets a wrong keep its full size and releases it anyway; excusing shrinks it to nothing. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew, Genesis 50:20: evil, harm. the word Joseph uses for what his brothers meant against him.

carryVoice: Your line: it wasn't okay. Both sentences can be true at once. That's day nine hundred seventy.
